passage: Shift supervisor's note, Gurleen, Friday. Recording this because I want to support it properly. On the evening shift the team has a habit of marking customer complaints 'resolved' after the first call so the numbers look good. Nirmala, our newest agent, has refused since her first week and calls customers back instead. Tonight in the break room, two senior agents called her 'Miss Too-Sincere' and 'not practical', loud enough for everyone. I watched her face drop for a second. Then she laughed and said, 'Practical is when the customer doesn't call back angry on Monday,' and showed them her repeat-call rate, the lowest on the floor. A couple of people laughed with her, not at her. Afterwards I told her privately that her method was right, and asked if she'd walk two new joiners through it next week. She looked relieved. I'll raise the 'resolved' habit at Monday's team meeting myself.

qa.q: What did the senior agents call Nirmala?
qa.a: They called her 'Miss Too-Sincere' and 'not practical'.

qa.q: What does Nirmala's face dropping for a second suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Nirmala felt hurt by the mockery before choosing to answer with humour.

qa.q: How did Nirmala hold her line without turning self-righteous?
qa.a: She answered with a joke and her low repeat-call rate, showing skill instead of preaching, and people laughed with her.

qa.q: How does Gurleen see Nirmala's method?
qa.a: Gurleen sees it as right and wants to spread it, asking Nirmala to train new joiners and raising the habit at the team meeting.

grounding: A supervisor's note records colleagues mocking an agent as too sincere for refusing a shortcut, and her holding the line with humour, skill and a new ally.

passage: Thursday. Baljeet's diary, site week six. Today at lunch Pawan called me 'Mr. Rulebook' again because I won't sign the scaffold checklist without climbing up to check the clamps. The whole crew laughed. My ears went red. I wanted to give a speech about the worker who fell at the Nashik site last year. I actually started one. Everyone's eyes glazed over and Pawan did a fake yawn. Worst move. After lunch, Minakshi, the other junior engineer, found me by the cement bags. 'Don't preach. Just be the one who's always right about the clamps.' Then she said she'd been checking hers properly too and getting the same jokes. So this afternoon, when Pawan called me Mr. Rulebook again, I bowed and said, 'At your service, and your clamp on level three is loose.' It was. He fixed it, grumbling. Minakshi and I are doing our checks together from Monday.

qa.q: What does Pawan call Baljeet?
qa.a: Pawan calls Baljeet 'Mr. Rulebook'.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling when the crew laughed?
qa.a: Baljeet felt hurt and embarrassed, ears going red, and wanted to lecture them.

qa.q: What worked better than the speech, and why?
qa.a: Answering with humour and skill by pointing out the loose clamp, because it held the line without preaching.

qa.q: What is it like for Minakshi, who faces the same jokes?
qa.a: Minakshi knows the sting too and offers to be Baljeet's ally, doing the checks together.

grounding: A diary shows a junior engineer mocked for refusing to skip safety checks, a preachy reaction that backfires, and then humour, skill and an ally.

passage: The bank branch in Madurai smelled of old files and phenyl. Rukmini sat across from the loan officer, Yusuf, with her admission letter for a nursing master's in Chennai and a form that felt thirty pages long. 'Just sign on the flags,' he said kindly. 'Everyone does.' Her hand hovered. Signing felt like chaining a rock to her ankles for years. She almost signed anyway, just to make the fear stop. Instead she asked, 'Can I take a copy home? I want to read the interest part, when repayment starts, and the total I'd pay back.' Yusuf nodded and printed a summary sheet. That night her aunt, who had repaid a loan for her own nursing degree, sat with her at the kitchen table. They compared the fees she actually needed with the amount on the form and crossed out the hostel extras her stipend could cover. On Monday Rukmini went back and asked for the smaller amount.

qa.q: What was Rukmini's admission letter for?
qa.a: It was for a nursing master's in Chennai.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling as her hand hovered over the form?
qa.a: Rukmini felt anxious and afraid, as if signing would chain her down for years.

qa.q: What did Rukmini do instead of signing out of anxiety?
qa.a: She took the summary home, read the key terms with her aunt, and went back to ask for only what she needed.

qa.q: How does Yusuf seem to see the signing?
qa.a: Yusuf sees it as routine, kindly saying everyone just signs, but he gives her a summary to read when asked.

grounding: Shows the fear of signing an education loan, and Rukmini reading the terms with a trusted adult and borrowing only what the course needs.

passage:
'The agent at the education fair said I just need to sign by Friday and the loan's approved,' Ganga said, spreading the papers on the bed.
Urmila, her elder cousin, picked up the top sheet. 'Did you read what the interest is?'
'I tried. My chest went tight and I stopped.'
'Okay. We'll read it together. Slowly.' Urmila ran a finger down the page. 'This part says repayment starts six months after the course ends. That's the moratorium.'
'And this?'
'That's what you'd pay back in total. See? Much more than the fee.'
Ganga went quiet. 'I didn't know it would be that much.'
'It might still be worth it. Your animation course has good placements. But look, they've added a laptop and a "lifestyle allowance". Do you need those?'
'I have a laptop.'
'Then cut them. Borrow what the course needs.'
Ganga circled the extras. 'Can we also ask the bank near college for their terms? Just to compare.'
'Now you're thinking.'

qa.q: When does repayment start, according to the page?
qa.a: Repayment starts six months after the course ends.

qa.q: How did Ganga feel when trying to read the interest part alone?
qa.a: Ganga felt anxious, her chest going tight, so she stopped reading.

qa.q: Which choices did Ganga make after reading with Urmila?
qa.a: Cutting the laptop and lifestyle extras she didn't need, and planning to compare terms with the bank near college.

qa.q: How does Urmila see the loan?
qa.a: Urmila thinks it may still be worth it for a course with good placements, but only if Ganga reads it and borrows what the course needs.

grounding: Shows anxiety about an education loan nearly leading to signing unread, and a cousin helping Ganga read the terms, compare and borrow only what is needed.

passage: Layla's mother had pawned her wedding gold in Amman to pay the first year of Layla's engineering fees in Manchester, and she mentioned it on almost every video call. 'Remember what we gave for this, habibti.' Layla always said she remembered. What she didn't say: she had failed the first thermodynamics exam and was retaking it in May. She hadn't told anyone but her flatmate, Freya. 'You're carrying two things,' Freya said one night, as Layla stared at a missed call. 'The exam, and the hiding. The hiding is heavier.' Layla called back. Her voice shook. 'Mama, I need to tell you something. I failed one exam. I'm retaking it in May, and I've booked extra tutorials. And when you remind me about the gold, I feel crushed. I know what you gave. I need you to trust me too.' Her mother was silent a long time. Then: 'Tell me about these tutorials.'

qa.q: What had Layla's mother pawned?
qa.a: Layla's mother had pawned her wedding gold.

qa.q: What was Layla feeling when her mother mentioned the gold?
qa.a: Layla felt crushed and guilty under the weight of the sacrifice.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Telling her mother about the failed exam, the plan for May and how the reminders felt, because it replaced hiding with honest planning.

qa.q: How might Layla's mother feel after hearing the truth?
qa.a: Her mother is shocked into silence at first, but then asks about the tutorials, perhaps relieved to be included.

grounding: Shows a daughter weighed down by her parents' pawned gold and reminders, and choosing to share her failure, her plan and the pressure instead of hiding.

passage: In the peer-mentoring room of the Warangal engineering college, Vijay finally said it aloud. 'My parents pledged Amma's jewellery at the bank for my fees. Nanna says it every time I call: "Her bangles are sitting in a locker because of you."' Eshaan, a final-year student who ran the Thursday sessions, waited. Vijay went on. 'I have two backlogs. I haven't told them. I keep saying everything's fine.' 'What would happen if you told them?' 'They'd be heartbroken.' 'And if they found out in May, from the result sheet?' Vijay stared at the table. Eshaan pulled out a sheet with the remedial class timings and exam dates, and together they wrote a plan. 'Now tell them the backlogs and the plan together,' Eshaan said. 'And tell them the reminders make it harder to study, not easier.' That evening Vijay called home from the hostel terrace. His father was quiet. Then he asked about the remedial class timings.

qa.q: How many backlogs does Vijay have?
qa.a: Vijay has two backlogs.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling when he kept saying everything was fine?
qa.a: Vijay felt guilty and afraid of breaking his parents' hearts, so he hid the backlogs.

qa.q: What did Eshaan help Vijay do?
qa.a: Write a dated plan with remedial classes and exams, then tell his parents the backlogs and the plan together, including how the reminders felt.

qa.q: How does Vijay's father respond to the truth?
qa.a: His father is quiet at first, then asks about the remedial class timings, showing he wants to help rather than blame.

grounding: Shows a student carrying guilt over his mother's pledged jewellery and hiding backlogs, and a peer mentor helping him speak honestly with a plan.

passage: Dhruv, put your phone down a minute. That app you've been looking at, the one that says 'cash in 10 minutes'? Let me, Devika, tell you what happened to me six years ago, when I was twenty-one. My scooter broke, and an app gave me money in minutes. No questions. A week later the calls began, twenty a day, rude voices. Then they messaged people from my contact list, saying I was a thief. My old school teacher got one. I wanted to crawl under the bed. I nearly took a second app loan to pay the first. My flatmate Sunita stopped me. 'Don't feed it. Screenshot everything.' She sat with me while I told my brother the whole thing. He helped me file a complaint on the government's cyber-crime portal and with the bank regulator's grievance line. The calls slowed, then stopped. Sorting it out took weeks. So, Dhruv: if a stranger's money comes that fast, ask why.

qa.q: Why did Devika borrow from the app?
qa.a: Devika's scooter broke.

qa.q: How did young Devika feel when her teacher got a message?
qa.a: Devika felt ashamed and trapped, wanting to crawl under the bed.

qa.q: What turning point in the story stopped things getting worse?
qa.a: Sunita stopping her from taking a second loan, then saving screenshots, telling her brother, and filing complaints through official channels.

qa.q: How might Sunita have felt seeing Devika about to take a second loan?
qa.a: Sunita was probably alarmed and protective, which is why she stepped in and stayed with Devika.

grounding: A senior colleague recalls an instant loan app's threats and shaming calls, and how stopping the borrowing, saving evidence, telling family and official complaints helped.

passage: It was the night before his final-year exam, and Sachin's phone would not stop. The loan app he had used for his hostel fees three weeks ago was calling every ten minutes, and now it had sent a message to his whole contact list: 'Sachin is a fraud. Call him.' His cousin forwarded it with a question mark. Sachin sat on the hostel stairs, hands shaking, thinking about taking a loan from another app just to make it stop. Instead he called his elder sister Vandana at 11 p.m. She listened to all of it without interrupting. 'Don't borrow again. Screenshot every message and call log right now. Tomorrow after your exam, we file a complaint on the cyber-crime portal and tell the bank. I'll message the family that it's a harassment scam.' She stayed on the phone while he saved the screenshots into a folder. Then she made him put the phone on silent and go to bed. He slept four hours, but he slept.

qa.q: What did the app send to Sachin's contact list?
qa.a: It sent the message 'Sachin is a fraud. Call him.'

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling on the hostel stairs?
qa.a: Sachin felt trapped and panicked, hands shaking, tempted to borrow again just to make it stop.

qa.q: Why are Vandana's steps wise?
qa.a: Stopping the borrowing, saving screenshots, filing an official complaint and warning the family breaks the cycle and builds a record.

qa.q: What might Sachin's cousin have thought on getting the message?
qa.a: The cousin was probably confused and worried, which is why the message came back with a question mark.

grounding: Shows an instant loan app shaming a student through his contacts on an exam night, and his sister's same-night help: no new borrowing, evidence and official complaints.

passage:
Week 1: Lokesh borrowed money from his roommate Manoj to pay for his mother's train ticket home. 'Pay whenever,' Manoj said. Lokesh promised the end of the month.
Week 5: The month ended. Lokesh's part-time pay was late. When Manoj's name flashed on his phone, Lokesh let it ring out. He started leaving for class before Manoj woke, eating at a different mess table. The embarrassment felt worse than the debt.
Week 7: Manoj left a note on his bed: 'Are we okay? I'm not angry about the money. I'm angry you disappeared.' Lokesh read it three times. That evening he sat on Manoj's bed. 'I'm sorry. My pay came late and I was too ashamed to say. I can give you half on the 5th and the rest on the 20th.' Manoj let out a breath. 'That's all I needed. Just tell me things.' They went for parottas, and Lokesh paid half on the 5th.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh borrow from Manoj?
qa.a: Lokesh borrowed to pay for his mother's train ticket home.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling in Week 5?
qa.a: Lokesh felt embarrassed and ashamed, which made him avoid Manoj.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do in Week 7 that repaired things?
qa.a: He apologised, explained honestly, and gave Manoj clear dates for paying back.

qa.q: What upset Manoj more than the money?
qa.a: Manoj was hurt that Lokesh disappeared, more than by the late repayment.

grounding: Shows embarrassment over a loan from a friend turning into avoidance, and honesty about what can be paid and when repairing the friendship.

passage: Gurleen, you say you're avoiding your friend because you owe her? Let old Tenzin from accounts tell you what that cost me. I was twenty, in Dharamshala, and I borrowed money from my best friend Dorjee for a secondhand bicycle for my delivery job. I promised to pay him in two months. Two months came and I didn't have it. So I stopped going to the tea shop where we met. I crossed the road when I saw him. I told myself I'd face him when I had the full amount. It took me eight months to gather it. By then he had moved to Delhi, and when I finally sent it, he wrote back one line: 'I never cared about the money.' We didn't speak for twelve years. If I had just said, 'Dorjee, I can give you a little each month,' I'd have kept my friend. So call her tonight, Gurleen. Tell her what you can pay and when.

qa.q: What did Tenzin buy with the borrowed money?
qa.a: Tenzin bought a secondhand bicycle for a delivery job.

qa.q: How did young Tenzin feel when two months passed without the money?
qa.a: Tenzin felt embarrassed and ashamed, which led to avoiding Dorjee.

qa.q: What choice inside the story would have saved the friendship?
qa.a: Telling Dorjee honestly, 'I can give you a little each month,' instead of avoiding him.

qa.q: What does Dorjee's one-line reply suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests Dorjee was hurt by the disappearance, not by the money.

grounding: An older colleague recalls dodging a friend out of embarrassment over a loan, and how avoidance cost the friendship more than the debt.

passage:
Dear Mohit,
I've typed and deleted this message many times, so I'm writing it properly instead.
In March I lent you money for your sister's college form. You said you'd return it by June. It's September now. I don't mind that it's late; things happen. What hurts is that you've stopped replying, and last week at Ravi's birthday you left the moment I walked in. I felt used, and then silly for feeling that.
I want to be plain with you, because I'd rather keep the friendship than keep quiet. Can you tell me what you're able to return, and by when? Even a small part and a date would help me stop worrying about it.
And whatever happens, from now on I'll only lend what I could easily let go of. That's not a punishment. It's just how I'll keep things simple between us.
Your friend,
Pooja

qa.q: By when did Mohit promise to return the money?
qa.a: Mohit said the money would be returned by June.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling when Mohit left the birthday party?
qa.a: Pooja felt used and hurt, then silly for feeling that way.

qa.q: Why is Pooja's letter a good way to ask?
qa.a: It asks plainly and kindly for an amount and a date, says what hurts, and sets a calm limit on future lending.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Mohit may feel ashamed but relieved to have a kind way back, rather than more avoiding.

grounding: A letter shows Pooja feeling used when a friend goes silent after borrowing, and asking plainly and kindly for a date while treating future loans as gifts.

passage: Here's something nobody tells you about lending money to a friend. I'm Alka, and last year I lent my college friend Kunal a chunk of my internship stipend when his laptop died before placements. He hugged me. Then he vanished. Not literally; he was still in every class. But he stopped sitting near me, stopped replying in the group, was suddenly always 'in a rush'. And I felt so awkward, as if I was the one who'd done something wrong. For two months I rehearsed speeches in the shower. Finally, one afternoon outside the library, I just said, 'Kunal, can we talk about the money? No drama. When do you think you can return it?' He went red. He said his first salary would come in July. We agreed on the 10th of July. He paid on the 12th, with a sheepish chocolate. And I decided that from now on I only lend what I could live without, as if it were a gift.

qa.q: Why did Kunal need the money?
qa.a: Kunal's laptop died before placements.

qa.q: How did Alka feel while Kunal was keeping away?
qa.a: Alka felt awkward and used, as if Alka were the one who had done something wrong.

qa.q: What finally worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking plainly and kindly outside the library and agreeing on a date, because it replaced avoidance with a clear plan.

qa.q: Why might Kunal have gone red when Alka asked?
qa.a: Kunal was probably embarrassed about avoiding Alka and not yet having the money.

grounding: A spoken account of a friend avoiding Alka after borrowing, the awkwardness of asking, and a plain, kind request with an agreed date.

passage: Counsellor's note, student wellness centre, Wednesday. Lalit, third-year commerce, came in with his roommate Anirban, who waited outside. Lalit said he had not slept properly in two weeks. He had been using a credit card so he could keep up with his friends' weekend plans, cafés, concert tickets, a trip to Goa, and paying only the smallest amount due each month. He did not know the total. He had told no one, not even Anirban, until last night. He kept saying, 'I'm so stupid,' and would not look up. I told him that shame makes people hide, and hiding lets these things grow. We opened the card statement together and he wrote the full figure on paper. He went pale, then oddly calmer. We agreed: he would cut up the card today, tell his elder brother this weekend, and meet the college's financial literacy volunteer on Friday to work out a repayment plan. I will check in with him on Monday.

qa.q: Who came in with Lalit?
qa.a: His roommate Anirban came in with him.

qa.q: What does Lalit repeating 'I'm so stupid' suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Lalit felt deep shame and self-blame about the hidden debt.

qa.q: What steps did the counsellor and Lalit agree on?
qa.a: Cut up the card, tell his elder brother, and meet the financial literacy volunteer to plan repayment.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Anirban to hear about it last night?
qa.a: Anirban was likely surprised and worried, and cared enough to bring Lalit in and wait outside.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a student hiding credit card overspending out of shame, then totalling it, stopping the spending, telling family and getting help with a plan.

passage: Sunday night. Ramesh, this is you writing to yourself so you stop lying. Tonight I finally added it up: every swipe since the office joining party in June. New phone, shoes to match everyone's, the weekend in Coorg I said yes to because I didn't want to be the one who couldn't. The total made me feel sick. I've been paying the minimum each month and telling myself it's fine. It isn't. I hid the statement under my mattress like a kid. Tonight I called Rehana-di. I expected a lecture. She just said, 'Okay. Thank you for telling me. Now we make a plan.' She's coming over on Tuesday to sit with me and the statement, and she said we'd call the bank together to ask what options exist. I've put the card in an envelope and given it to my flatmate to hold. First weekend in months I'm not going anywhere. Weirdly, I feel lighter.

qa.q: Where did Ramesh hide the statement?
qa.a: Ramesh hid the statement under the mattress.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling when the total was added up?
qa.a: Ramesh felt sick with shame after hiding the debt for months.

qa.q: What steps did Ramesh take tonight, and why do they help?
qa.a: Telling Rehana-di, planning to go through the statement and call the bank together, and handing the card to the flatmate, which ends the hiding and the spending.

qa.q: How does Rehana-di respond to Ramesh's call?
qa.a: Rehana-di responds calmly and warmly, thanking Ramesh for telling and moving to a plan instead of a lecture.

grounding: A diary shows hidden credit card overspending to keep up with friends, and Ramesh totalling it, stopping the spending and telling someone safe.

passage:
'You're taking a loan from that app? For the deposit?' Afreen stared at the phone screen.
'It's just three weeks, until my first salary comes.'
'Sarika, look at the charges. That's a lot for three weeks.'
'I know. But I'm not calling Mama-ji. I told everyone I'd manage Bengaluru on my own.'
'Mama-ji offered in April. He said, "Just ask."'
'And then at every wedding he'll say he paid for my flat.'
'Will he? Or is that your pride talking?'
Sarika was quiet. 'Maybe a bit of both.'
'Being independent is great. But paying all that extra to look independent isn't independence.'
'So I just ask?'
'You ask for exactly the deposit, you tell him the date you'll return it, and you return it. That's still you managing.'
Sarika looked at the app's red 'Apply now' button for a long moment. Then she closed it and scrolled to Mama-ji's number.

qa.q: How long does Sarika need the money for?
qa.a: Sarika needs it for three weeks, until the first salary comes.

qa.q: What is Sarika worried about in asking Mama-ji?
qa.a: Sarika feels proud and wary, afraid he will say at every wedding that he paid for the flat.

qa.q: What middle path does Afreen suggest?
qa.a: Ask Mama-ji for exactly the deposit, give a return date and repay it, instead of paying heavy charges to protect an image.

qa.q: How might Mama-ji see a request for help?
qa.a: Mama-ji offered in April and said 'Just ask', so he may be glad to be asked rather than seeing it as weakness.

grounding: Shows pride in looking self-made nearly leading to a costly loan, and a friend helping Sarika see a short family bridge as the sensible choice.

passage: I'm Sharmila, and I paid a lot to protect an image nobody was looking at. When my scooter was stolen in my first year of work in Pune, I needed another one to reach the site office. My aunt, Alka-masi, had offered to help with anything. I said no. I wanted to be the one in the family who never needed anyone. So I took a quick loan from a finance shop near the station, with charges I barely read. For eleven months I paid it back, skipping dinners out and a trip home for Diwali. Last month, over chai, I told Alka-masi the whole story. She put her cup down. 'You could have borrowed from me and paid me back in a few months. I'd have been proud you asked.' I felt foolish, then oddly relieved. I'm still proud of standing on my own feet. I've just learnt that a short bridge from family isn't the same as falling.

qa.q: What did Sharmila need a new scooter for?
qa.a: Sharmila needed it to reach the site office.

qa.q: What did Sharmila feel when Alka-masi said she'd have been proud?
qa.a: Sharmila felt foolish and then oddly relieved.

qa.q: What lesson did Sharmila take about pride and help?
qa.a: Standing on one's own feet is good, but a short, honest bridge from family beats paying heavy charges to protect an image.

qa.q: How does Alka-masi see Sharmila's refusal to ask?
qa.a: Alka-masi would have been proud to be asked and seems a little saddened that Sharmila struggled alone.

grounding: A first-person look back at refusing family help to seem self-made and paying heavy charges instead, and learning when a short bridge is sensible.

passage: Indu was at the crowded Friday vegetable market in Jaipur, a bag of tomatoes in one hand, when her phone rang. 'Indu Sharma? This is your bank's security team. Your account is being used for a suspicious transfer right now. To block it, I'm sending an OTP. Read it back to me in the next two minutes.' The man knew her name and her bank. Her heart hammered; her whole first salary was in that account. The vendor was shouting prices, a scooter honked, and the voice kept saying, 'Madam, hurry.' Her phone buzzed with the OTP. Then she remembered what her friend Ayesha had said after her own close call: real banks never ask for an OTP. 'I'll call my branch myself,' Indu said, and hung up. Her hands were shaking. She stepped behind a stall and dialled the number printed on the back of her debit card. The bank said her account was fine and asked her to report the caller's number, which she did.

qa.q: Where was Indu when the call came?
qa.a: Indu was at the crowded Friday vegetable market in Jaipur.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling when the caller said her account was being used?
qa.a: Indu felt frightened, her heart hammering, because her whole first salary was in that account.

qa.q: Which choice protected Indu, and why?
qa.a: Hanging up and calling the number on the back of her card, because it checked through an official channel and kept the OTP private.

qa.q: How did Ayesha's own close call help Indu?
qa.a: Ayesha had learned that real banks never ask for an OTP, and passing that on gave Indu the pause she needed.

grounding: Shows a scam caller posing as the bank using fear and urgency in a noisy market, and Indu pausing, hanging up and verifying through official channels.

passage: The call came while Zeenat was ironing her one good kurta in their Lucknow flat. 'Congratulations, Zeenat Ansari. You've been shortlisted for airport ground staff. The final list closes at 5 p.m. today. Just share the OTP I'm sending, to verify your registration.' He knew her name, her college and the job portal she had used. After four months of rejections, her heart leapt. She was reaching for the phone to read the number out when her cousin Jasleen, sitting on the bed, mouthed, 'Wait.' Zeenat put the call on hold. 'Why would a real airline need your OTP?' Jasleen asked. 'And why the hurry?' Zeenat's hope curdled into a cold feeling. She hung up. Together they looked up the airline's official careers page: no such drive listed. Jasleen helped her block the number and report it on the national cyber-crime helpline website. Zeenat sat down on the bed, disappointed and angry, but with her account safe.

qa.q: By what time did the caller say the list would close?
qa.a: The caller said the final list closes at 5 p.m. today.

qa.q: What happened to Zeenat's hope when Jasleen asked her questions?
qa.a: Zeenat's hope turned into a cold feeling of fear and suspicion.

qa.q: What steps did Zeenat and Jasleen take after hanging up?
qa.a: They checked the airline's official careers page, blocked the number, and reported it on the cyber-crime helpline website.

qa.q: How does Jasleen see the call?
qa.a: Jasleen sees the OTP request and the rush as warning signs of a scam.

grounding: Shows a fake job agent using Zeenat's hope and a deadline to ask for an OTP, and a cousin helping her pause, verify and report.

passage: Raghav stood in the placement office of his Bhopal college at 9 a.m., eyes red. Last night he had paid the 'training deposit' for a remote data-entry job, three months of his savings from tutoring, to a company that had interviewed him on video and sent an offer on letterhead. This morning the number was switched off and the website was gone. 'I'm so stupid,' he told Tanuja, the placement officer. 'Everyone will laugh.' Tanuja shook her head. 'These people are professionals. They target people who are hoping. That's not stupidity.' She pushed a phone toward him. 'Call the cyber-crime helpline now. Speed matters.' He did, with shaking hands, and read out the transaction details. She helped him file the online complaint too. Then he called his father. At noon, Tanuja asked if she could share his story, without his name, in the placement group. He hesitated, then agreed. By evening two juniors had written in: they had received the same 'offer'.

qa.q: What did Raghav pay last night?
qa.a: Raghav paid the 'training deposit' for a remote data-entry job.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling in the placement office?
qa.a: Raghav felt humiliated and foolish, afraid everyone would laugh.

qa.q: Which steps did Raghav take, and why did speed matter?

passage:
Dear Ojas,
You asked why I went quiet last month. Here's the truth, and please share it with your batch.
I got a message about a work-from-home job rating hotel reviews. The first two tasks paid small amounts into my account, so it felt real. Then they said I had to 'upgrade' by depositing money to unlock bigger tasks. I deposited, then deposited again, chasing the promised returns, until my savings from two summers of tutoring were gone. The group chat vanished overnight.
I felt so stupid I didn't eat for a day. My sister found me and made me call the cyber-crime helpline that same evening. We filed complaints online and at the bank. I don't know if I'll get anything back.
What I've learnt: these people are organised and they aim at hope, not at fools. If anyone asks you to pay in order to earn, stop, and tell someone.
Take care,
Divyansh

qa.a: The job was rating hotel reviews.

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel after the group chat vanished?
qa.a: Divyansh felt humiliated and stupid, too upset to eat for a day.

qa.q: What does Divyansh advise others to do?
qa.a: Stop if anyone asks you to pay in order to earn, and tell someone.

qa.q: How did Divyansh's sister help that day?
qa.a: She made Divyansh call the cyber-crime helpline that same evening and helped file complaints, instead of letting shame delay it.

grounding: A letter shares the story of losing savings to a fake job scam, reporting it the same day with family help, and warning others that scams target hope.
